legacy.text: The emergency currency the order helped staff for was issued only once, in 1914–1915: $382,502,645 to 1,363 banks, all retired without loss by December 1915.
legacy.source: Comptroller of the Currency, Annual Report, 1915

legacy.text: The National Monetary Commission created by the same law reported the Aldrich Plan on January 8, 1912; the Federal Reserve Act followed on December 23, 1913.

related.note: Waived, for Treasury hires under the currency law, Civil Service Rule VIII as amended by EO 741.

later_actions.text: Section 27 of the Federal Reserve Act extended the Aldrich–Vreeland emergency-currency provisions to June 30, 1915.

political_impact.text: Charles Jonathan Arnell became assistant Japanese secretary at Tokyo on June 25, 1908, and Willys Ruggles Peck assistant Chinese secretary at Peking on November 9, 1908.
political_impact.source: Register of the Department of State

uncertain: Whether Executive Order 829 actually prescribes filling the posts "in rotation" is not known; its text has not been found.

legacy.text: Basil Miles ran the foreign mail service until 1913 and then returned to the State Department.

reception.text: The San Juan Islander reported that Royal Vancouver Yacht Club yachts could now visit Puget Sound ports without entry, clearance or charges, under the act of May 28.

legacy.text: The reciprocity provision behind the order was later codified and remained the basis for excusing foreign yacht-club vessels from entry and clearance.

uncertain: The text of Executive Order 831 has not been found.
A Royal Vancouver skipper won the Alexandra Cup from the Seattle defender Spirit within two weeks, but no record ties the order to the races.

related.note: Allowed the New York customs district a second excepted paymaster in Schedule A.

political_impact.text: Apart from the yacht order, none of these orders drew recorded public notice.
